The real story here is that enterprises finally figured out you don't need to buy every shiny AI thing that launches, which is refreshingly sensible.

digital-culture.title: The economy is adding jobs—but more Americans are stuck working part-time
digital-culture.excerpt: Hiring in October blew past expectations, with U.S. employers adding 165,000 jobs and unemployment edging down to 4.1%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) also revised its jobs estimates upward for
digital-culture.dwp_take: The U.S. job market added 165,000 positions in October with unemployment holding at 4.1%, but the BLS quietly revealed more people are working part-time involuntarily rather than by choice. This matters because it signals your workforce planning assumptions might be off, your team's actual earning capacity is shrinking, and retention becomes harder when people need secondary gigs. digital-culture.title: The hidden cost of workplace transformation: How change initiatives crush top employees
digital-culture.excerpt: Nearly half of employees report experiencing "transformation fatigue," according to a recent study
digital-culture.dwp_take:
Here's the response:

A new study found that nearly half of employees are burned out from constant workplace transformation initiatives. This matters because digital workplace leaders are often the architects pushing these changes, yet they're frequently blind to the cumulative toll on their best people, who tend to absorb extra work during transitions. After three decades in this space, I can tell you that "transformation fatigue" is just a fancy term for what used to be called "we changed everything again without asking anyone," and it's still killing productivity just as effectively as it did in 1995.

digital-culture.title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
digital-culture.excerpt: Data brokers are collecting all sorts of internal corporate files to help train AI models. Not everyone is thrilled.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Data brokers are quietly harvesting internal corporate documents and emails to train AI models, and most companies haven't even noticed it's happening. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it's a direct threat to information governance, compliance, and the whole reason you built those access controls in the first place. Here's the thing: we spent twenty years teaching people not to email passwords, and now we're basically leaving the whole filing cabinet unlocked while data brokers fill their trucks out back.
